fixes.explanation: The sea it is, friend! Paul says the forefathers were all under the cloud and that they all passed through the sea (1 Corinthians 10:1). Notice the word ALL. Not some, not most, ALL of them went through.

Christ it is! Paul says they drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Read that slowly, friend. The rock went along with them. And what they drank from it was the same spiritual drink for all of them.

Aaron doesn't appear anywhere in this passage, friend. The only leader Paul names is Moses, when he says they were baptized into Moses (1 Corinthians 10:2). The rock is a different matter, and Paul names it directly: it was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4).

The cloud is in this passage, but Paul isn't giving a reason for it here. He says, “These things took place as examples to keep us from craving evil things as they did.” (1 Corinthians 10:6). His point is the examples, friend. They're there to keep us from craving evil things.

That's the one! Paul writes, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). Then he backs it up with a line from Scripture: “The people sat down to eat and drink and got up to indulge in revelry.” He sets the warning right beside the example, friend.

Paul doesn't use the word greedy there, friend. His first warning is, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). The line he uses to back it up is about people sitting down to eat and drink and getting up to indulge in revelry. That line goes with idolatry, so greed isn't the word to look for.

Lazy isn't in the verse, friend. Paul says, “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.” (1 Corinthians 10:7). Look at the line he backs it with: the people sat down to eat and drink, then got up to indulge in revelry. Nobody in that line is lounging around, so the warning to hold onto is idolaters.

Paul doesn't say lie in this list, friend. The fourth warning is, “And do not complain, as some of them did, and were killed by the destroying angel.” (1 Corinthians 10:10). It's a heavy line, and the word to remember is complain.

Paul doesn't say stop, friend. He writes, “So the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall.” (1 Corinthians 10:12). Standing firm and falling are the pair here, and the warning is for the one who feels steady. Feeling steady is exactly when to watch your step.

An escape is right, friend! Paul says, “But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Just before that he says, “And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.” So God is the one who provides it, and the point is that you can stand up under the temptation.

A reward isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, “But when you are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you can stand up under it.” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Right before that he says “He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.” The promise is about getting through the temptation, not about a prize.

Standing against it sounds brave, friend, but Paul uses a different word. He writes, “Therefore, my beloved, flee from idolatry.” (1 Corinthians 10:14). Flee means get away from it, not square up to it. Just before this he warns that the one who thinks he is standing firm should be careful not to fall (1 Corinthians 10:12).

Paul doesn't say kings, friend. He writes, “…the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God.” (1 Corinthians 10:20). Then he adds, “And I do not want you to be participants with demons.” Kings don't come into it. His worry is about taking part with demons.

A temple isn't what Paul names, friend. He puts a cup beside a cup first, then a table beside a table (1 Corinthians 10:21). Each time it's the Lord's on one side and demons' on the other, and he says you can't have both. That makes the second thing a table.

Jealousy is right, friend. Paul asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). He asks it right after saying you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too (1 Corinthians 10:21). Then he follows with a second question: “Are we stronger than He?”

Sorrow isn't the word, friend. Paul asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). He asks it right after saying you cannot have the Lord's table and the table of demons too (1 Corinthians 10:21). So the question is about mixing the two, and what he names is jealousy.

Mercy would be a gentler word, friend, but Paul's question names something else. He asks, “Are we trying to provoke the Lord to jealousy?” (1 Corinthians 10:22). It comes right after his words about the cup and the table of the Lord and of demons (1 Corinthians 10:21). The word that finishes the question is jealousy.
